title: We turned one 5-second AI-generated clip into six pixel sprite sequences. Here's what needed manual cleanup.
author: daetz4812
selftext:
We tried putting six AI-generated units in a single Wan clip, then turning that clip into separate sprite sequences. The experiment was about whether batching still leaves you with poses you can use in a game.

We laid the units out in a 3×2 grid on solid magenta, with the same foot anchor in each cell and room around their weapons. In SpriteFrame, we imported the clip and the grid JSON, keyed out the magenta, and extracted 900 candidate frames across the six units at the source frame rate. At 10 fps that was 50 candidates per unit. The hammer strike in the last image uses 12 selected frames.

The grid made cropping repeatable. It couldn't fix a weapon crossing a cell boundary or colored fringes from video compression, so we reviewed the motion at game scale in Godot and picked the poses by hand. We used Pixel Frog's Tiny Swords as a style reference; the six generated units are ours.

We released the SpriteFrame code under MIT and the original example sprite sheets under CC0. The sample clip and grid JSON are included if you want to reproduce the extraction: [https://daetz-coder.github.io/projects/pixel-asset-workshop/](https://daetz-coder.github.io/projects/pixel-asset-workshop/)

For anyone who has tried video-to-sprite workflows: how do you handle fast weapon swings? Do you leave a wider margin around each unit or generate the weapon motion on a separate layer?
